The analysis focused on the period between 2003 and 2022 in the Netherlands, where strong editorial safeguards coexist with high media concentration. Findings showed that reporting on media mergers focused primarily on who owns the media and why, rather than on broader implications for the news market. Outlets used significantly more justifying frames when covering mergers involving their owner compared to when the owner was not involved. No difference was found for criticizing frames. Furthermore, while the Dutch market became increasingly concentrated, recent mergers featured more justifying but not fewer criticizing frames. Similarly, outlets undergoing takeovers engaged in more justification, while criticism was unaffected. Overall, the results call for a reconsideration of the presumed resilience of journalistic autonomy against corporate pressures in democratic markets.

latest.title: Pressured by the Comments? Chinese Journalists in the Face of Online Violence
latest.abstract: In the increasingly digital context of China’s public sphere, journalists frequently encounter online violence that threatens their professional autonomy, emotional wellbeing, and freedom of expression. Drawing on 20 semi-structured interviews with journalists representing a cross section of the Chinese media landscape, this study identifies four major types of online violence experienced by Chinese journalists: violence in response to alleged unprofessional behaviours, violence based on moral coercion, violence motivated by so-called “nationalism”, and gendered violence. Cultural norms, nationalist ideologies, and patriarchy emerge as key factors shaping and underpinning online violence. With regard to journalists’ coping strategies, these are found to include individualised and emotionally taxing approaches, such as silence, avoidance and contempt, while institutional support is either limited in its responsiveness or sometimes unavailable. This study provides an enhanced understanding of the role of online violence in shaping journalistic practice and coping strategies in a highly interactive and emotional digital media environment. The findings indicate that online violence driven by wider structural and cultural forces, is becoming an increasingly common informal control mechanism, undermining journalistic authority and autonomy and therefore the stability and sustainability of journalism itself.

latest.title: News is Becoming Similar? A Diachronic Text Mining Exploration of News Convergence in Chinese Media
latest.abstract: The convergence of news has long been a central concern in media studies, yet empirical evidence and precise measurements remain limited. China’s unique media system, which operates simultaneously in domestic and global contexts under distinct communication strategies, offers a rare opportunity to advance this line of inquiry. This study draws on news posts (N = 607,871) from four leading Chinese outlets over the past decade and applies a text-mining approach to examine Chinese news convergence across the two contexts and its relationship with audience news engagement. The results show a significant increase in lexical similarity among Chinese media in the global context but not in the domestic context. No upward trend in thematic structural similarity is observed in either context. Moreover, the associations between convergence and audience engagement are context-dependent: in the domestic context, lexical similarity is negatively associated with engagement, whereas in the global context, both lexical and thematic similarity are positively associated with engagement. These results challenge conventional views of news convergence, highlighting its dynamic nature across temporal and contextual dimensions. Further implications for theory and practice are discussed.

latest.title: Satire in Exile: Exiled Newsfluencers' use of Satire as a Discursive Strategy
latest.abstract: This article examines how one newsfluencer in exile employs satire as a discursive strategy to sustain counter-publics in autocratic contexts. Through a multimodal critical discourse analysis of twenty videos by Stephen Shiu, a prominent Hong Kong newsfluencer now based in Taiwan, this article identifies a range of satirical strategies used in his commentary, including irony, exaggeration, parody, mock expertise, profanity, insult, metaphor, rumour, and personal anecdote. Drawing from these findings, we discuss how, in this case, satirists in exile may help provide critical information when domestic journalism is silenced, articulate collective frustration through emotional expression, and preserve local Cantonese profanity as a form of identity politics. This article adds to the literature on satire and social media by showing that online platforms like YouTube provide newsfluencers in exile with greater freedom of expression than would have been possible in legacy media, as well as sustain critical journalism in exile.

latest.title: Future Problems, Present Challenges: Exploring Journalistic Practices and the Normative Role of Journalism in Reporting Persistent Social Issues
“If No One Is Doing Anything, What’s the Point of Hearing about It Again and Again?” Youth, Climate Journalism and Mediated Public (Dis)connection
latest.abstract: For news media, climate journalism has been identified as both a normative responsibility and a strategic beat for reaching young audiences. This paper examines whether and how news media shape engagement with and public connection to climate change among Norwegian youth. Drawing on an in-depth qualitative study of 33 participants in a high-choice, digitally advanced media environment, I analyse the place of climate journalism in everyday media repertoires of youth. Prior engagement is decisive: climate issues are salient for already-concerned youth, but largely absent among others. Across groups, news media are not primary sources for climate information or engagement, suggesting that news-centric audience research may overstate news media’s role in public engagement with climate change and overlook youth-specific media habits. Combining different mediated public connection frameworks, the study shows why news media often fail to connect young people to climate change as a public issue. It introduces two interrelated analytical concepts: a lack of spatiotemporally grounded solutions in news coverage, which can lead to informed disconnection, a form of public disconnection with climate change partly produced by, rather than resolved by, climate journalism. Further, it proposes practice-oriented recommendations.

latest.title: Survival Tactics: Investigative Journalism Methods Under Threats and Barriers in Kazakhstan
latest.abstract: Investigative journalists face growing legal, physical, psychological, and institutional pressures that shape how investigations are conducted. While prior research has documented risks to journalists, little empirical work has examined how different threats reconfigure investigative methods, particularly in Kazakhstan. This study addresses this gap through semi-structured interviews with 13 investigative journalists. The findings show that risk does not lead to the abandonment of investigative practices but to method-specific adaptations. Legal threats encourage the use of legally defensible approaches such as open-source research, official documents, data journalism, and collaboration, while discouraging anonymous sources and undercover work. Physical threats shift investigations toward remote and digitally mediated practices. Psychological pressure favors emotionally sustainable, analytical methods, and structural barriers limit access to official information, prompting reliance on independent data reconstruction and verification. By linking specific threats to distinct methodological responses, the study offers an empirically grounded framework for understanding how risk reshapes investigative journalism in Kazakhstan.

latest.title: Facebook Community Standards: The New Gatekeeper for Palestinian News Organizations?
latest.abstract: This study examines how Facebook’s Community Standards act as a “gatekeeper” in ways that shape the editorial practices of Palestinian news organizations. It investigates how Facebook’s policies and algorithms influence their coverage of Palestine and the Israeli occupation. Findings reveal that these organizations navigate platform censorship by altering content and turning to platforms like Telegram to avoid restrictions, highlighting the tension between freedom of speech and maintaining visibility under digital constraints.

latest.title: Under Construction: Democracy Reporting as Paradigm Repair
latest.abstract: In recent years, several news organizations in the United States have added a new beat to their newsrooms: the democracy beat. In this study, we analyze the metajournalistic discourse about the creation of teams tasked with democracy-specific reporting. We contribute to scholarship about the relationship between democracy and journalism at a time when both are under duress. The creation of democracy beats, we find, is a critique of political reporting as usual and an exercise in both paradigm repair and paradigm renewal. News outlets are trying to rehabilitate the normative role of journalists as watchdogs and defenders of democracy. Democracy desks are expected to adopt a more adversarial approach and critical standpoint as they challenge the objectivity paradigm. This study provides valuable insights into the institutional response of U.S. news organizations at the local, state, and national levels to attacks on the free press and to the escalating anti-media rhetoric putting journalism’s institutional role in a democratic society to the test.

latest.title: Growing Inequalities Through Motivations: A Moderated Mediation Analysis Between Socioeconomic Status, Political Interest and News Media Consumption in Sweden, 1990–2023
latest.abstract: As we have transitioned toward media systems increasingly characterized by proliferation of media choices, public and scholarly concern regarding widening news consumption gaps have grown. Two types of gaps have been especially prominent in research on news audience fragmentation. The first is research building on the opportunity, motivation and abilities (OMA) framework, showing that individual motivations and preferences are becoming more important when it comes to news consumption. The second is research focused on how high-choice media environments might contribute to socioeconomic (SES) gaps in news consumption. We know from previous research that these two gaps are related since SES shapes political interest through socialization processes, which in turn drives news consumption. However, previous research lacks an integrated longitudinal perspective, testing whether this mediated relationship has increased over time. Addressing these shortcomings, we utilize 33 years of Swedish survey data (NRespondents = 47 884) to conduct a moderated mediation analysis, simultaneously studying the direct effect of socioeconomic status as well as its indirect – mediated through political interest – effect on news consumption. Results suggest that socioeconomic gaps in news consumption have grown and that an important driver of these differences might be due to an increasing indirect effect through political interest.

latest.title: The Somatechnic Hermeneutic: “Embodying” the Worlds of Journalism Study
latest.abstract: This study introduces a somatechnic hermeneutic to bridge the theoretical insights of the bodily turn in journalism studies with the empirical architecture of large-scale survey research, exemplified by the Worlds of Journalism Study (WJS). We argue that indicators such as safety, autonomy, precarity, and role conceptions are not merely abstract variables but proxies for lived, embodied experience. Applying this hermeneutic to Portugal's paradoxical profile–marked by high physical safety alongside acute economic precarity–we identify a state of somatic dissonance, in which the journalistic body is caught between physical protection and systemic strain. Through comparative analysis, we demonstrate how this dissonance fractures professional self-perception, revealing that professional role commitments are not only cognitive ideals but also corporeal practices. This approach re-frames perceptual survey data into a narrative of embodied experience and provides a framework for addressing empirical paradoxes, offering a transferable methodology for understanding how the pressures of journalism are somatically registered and endured across diverse media systems.

latest.title: Journalists in a Multicrisis Situation: External Crises as Accelerators of Long-Term Internal Crises and a Lost Opportunity for Resilience Building
latest.abstract: Recent crises epitomise the current age of disruption within journalism. Journalism faces a multicrisis situation, where internal issues—mainly economic and technological—accumulate with external predicaments, such as the COVID-19 pandemic, or the war in Ukraine, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. From the perspective of resilience building, such disruptions may represent not only threats but also opportunities for change and adaptation. To explore journalists’ interpretations of the relationship between their occupation and large societal crises, we conducted in-depth interviews to show how journalists perceive the disruptions of their work and how they build their professional resilience, focusing on a specific context of a post-transformation Central European country, the Czech Republic. Our findings suggest that large external crises are perceived as accelerators for long-term internal crises in the profession, which, due to the lack of deep collective reflection, represent a wasted opportunity for systemic change. Instead, they push professionals into individualised solutions and highlight the conflict between their social responsibility and the economic pressures of competitiveness.

latest.title: Effects of Infotainment Features in Instagram News Stories on Knowledge: A Field Experiment
latest.abstract: Instagram has become a relevant platform for news consumption. Therefore, it is crucial to understand how characteristics of Instagram news stories affect learning. A field experiment was conducted to investigate the effects of typical Instagram infotainment features—interaction, dynamic elements, and narration—on knowledge about current affairs. Participants (n = 350) followed a manipulated Instagram account for a week and then completed a knowledge test. Overall, exposure to the Instagram stories had a positive effect on knowledge; participants in all experimental conditions had higher knowledge than participants in the control group. This differs from previous findings related to other social media news, for example on Facebook. However, the infotainment features did not affect tracked exposure to the news stories or learning from the news. Moreover, they did not lead to entertainment experiences, which questions underlying assumptions about infotainment.

latest.title: Is Digitization Turning the Inverted Pyramid Upside Down? A Longitudinal Analysis of a Hundred Years of News Storytelling
latest.abstract: The inverted pyramid model for structuring news articles, according to which the most important facts are presented in the lead sentence, can be regarded as a cornerstone of journalism. In this longitudinal study, news articles from various German media were analyzed over a 100-year period. Automated content analysis was applied to a large corpus of German news articles published between 1924 and 2024 to detect whether the so-called 5W1H-questions were answered at the beginning of the news stories. We focused on the prominence of the concrete facts what, who, when, where, without coding for why and how. This was complemented by a qualitative analysis of semistructured interviews with journalists from three generations, to contextualize and interpret the longitudinal quantitative findings. According to the results, the news structure remained stable both in media practice and in journalists’ perceptions of how news should be structured throughout the twentieth century. However, in the digital era this news structure appears to be under pressure. The findings suggest that while the inverted pyramid model remained remarkably resilient across different political regimes of the twentieth century, its dominance has begun to fluctuate in the context of a shifting media ecosystem and probably new business models online.

latest.title: Reworking Journalism at the Digital Periphery: Role Work among Political Creators
latest.abstract: Political creators have become central actors in contemporary public communication and increasingly perform functions traditionally associated with journalism. Their growing presence has blurred the boundaries between journalism and its environment, raising questions about how journalistic roles are reworked beyond institutional newsrooms. Journalism studies have responded to these blurred boundaries through research on boundary negotiations, professional norms, and journalistic authority, largely from the perspective of the journalistic center. This article shifts the focus toward the periphery and examines how digitally enabled actors position themselves in relation to journalism and create their roles vis-à-vis the journalistic center. To conceptualize these peripheral perspectives, the article introduces the concept of role work and explores the concept in an exploratory empirical study. Drawing on 22 qualitative interviews with German political creators, the study shows that creators neither fully adopt nor categorically reject journalistic role models. Instead, they engage in selective, hybrid, and context-sensitive reinterpretations of journalistic values, goals, and practices. These processes of role work are shaped by platform affordances, small-scale production outside newsroom structures, the experienced boundary work of the journalistic center, and close, interactive relationships with audiences.

latest.title: What Keeps Journalists Going: Exploring Portuguese Journalists’ Subjective Well-being
When Journalists Speak: Media Framing and Accountability in Gender Representation Policies in Ghana
latest.abstract: Journalists play a role in shaping public perception, especially by holding political figures accountable for their promises. Drawing on critical discourse analysis and framing theory, the qualitative case study analyzes a purposively selected corpus of 14 news articles and one video from diverse Ghanaian media platforms to assess how media narratives challenge political leadership or reinforce existing power structures. Specifically, this study examines how selected Ghanaian media outlets framed discourse surrounding the President’s promise to ensure 30% representation of women in cabinet and ministerial positions. It highlights how, in this case, journalists in Ghana subtly advocated by quoting civil society actors, political figures, and legal references while appearing to maintain objectivity. The paper interrogates the media’s selective attention to gender-related political promises, contributing to scholarship on journalistic role conception, gender politics, and media accountability in emerging democracies.

latest.title: The Limited Power of Journalists: Insights from the Armstrong Case on the Social Conditions Enabling the Neutralisation of Investigative Reporting
latest.abstract: This study examines how power relations can hinder journalistic investigations when it targets an actor with high symbolic, economic, and social capital. It is based on an investigation conducted by Damien Ressiot in 2005, a journalist with L’Équipe, France’s leading sports newspaper, which provided evidence of doping by cyclist Lance Armstrong. Although the evidence was irrefutable, the investigation was contested and turned against its author, who found himself facing public accusations. Combining Bourdieu’s theoretical framework with Goffman’s frame analysis, we explore the mechanisms that enabled Armstrong to impose a favourable interpretative framework and neutralise the investigation’s impact. Our analysis is based on a rich empirical corpus (official reports, journalistic literature, and press articles) and complemented by several interviews with Ressiot. We show that Armstrong relied on a broad coalition of actors, made possible by his exceptional symbolic capital and central position in the cycling economy. Ressiot, by contrast, had very limited support, even within his own editorial team, leading to the symbolic disqualification of his work. As very few studies have addressed or conceptualised the issue of neutralising journalistic investigation, this article contributes to a wider understanding of the effects of power concentration on journalistic investigation.

latest.title: “Hewers of Wood and Drawers of Water”: Power Dynamics in Transnational Collaborative Investigative Journalism
latest.abstract: The article examines power imbalances in global collaborative investigative journalism networks that connect journalists from the Global South and North. These collaborations are praised for promoting global transparency and holding elites accountable, yet the power dynamics within them remain underexplored. Drawing on in-depth interviews with investigative journalists across Africa, the article examines how unequal power relations manifest and what factors drive them. Two key factors are identified: the challenging conditions of African newsroom infrastructures and the continued practice of “parachute journalism” by Global North newsrooms during global collaborations. The absence of an inclusive global journalism structure governing these networks exacerbates these imbalances, often leaving African journalists in subordinate roles. The paper contributes to the growing literature on transnational collaborative journalism, highlighting the need for more equitable structures in these global networks.

latest.title: Are Cherry Blossoms DC’s Polar Bears? Investigating the Links Between Local Seasonal Climate Journalism and Equity in Washington, DC
“Watching the Watchdogs Attacked”: Audience Perception of Online Harassment of Journalists in Kenya
latest.abstract: While research documents how online harassment affects journalists, far less is known about how audiences interpret and respond to such attacks. This study addresses this gap through 19 semi-structured, in-depth interviews with Kenyan adults from urban and rural areas. We examine how audiences in Kenya describe encounters with online harassment of journalists (OHJ), explain its causes, and respond when they witness it. Findings indicate that audiences often interpret OHJ through political and moral lenses, attributing it to journalists’ perceived political affiliations, professional conduct, reporting practices, or failure to meet public expectations of journalistic norms. Participants also point to broader structural drivers, including political polarization, normalized digital hostility, coordinated online campaigns, and gendered abuse such as trolling and sexualized attacks. Audience responses varied, with some engaging in counter-speech and public defense, while others withdrew due to fear of retaliation or feelings of powerlessness.

latest.title: Avoiding the News But Still Feeling Connected? The Role of News Use and Avoidance Practices in Different Public Connection Repertoires
latest.abstract: While current research acknowledges the existence of various forms of news avoidance, less attention has been paid to how these forms relate to the different ways individuals engage with public spheres. This study builds on the concept of public connection repertoires—structured patterns of practices through which individuals relate to different publics. Drawing on qualitative interviews and contextualized repertoire maps conducted in Germany between 2019 and 2022, we develop an empirical typology of public connection repertoires and examine the role of news use and news avoidance within them. The analysis includes communicative practices relevant to public connection beyond hard news consumption, such as interpersonal communication. As different forms of news avoidance appear across the full spectrum of public connection repertoires, our findings suggest that avoiding the news does not necessarily indicate disengagement from public life. In this context, the repertoire approach offers a more nuanced understanding of the multifaceted nature of news avoidance and its democratic implications.

latest.title: Constructive or Constrained? Solutions Journalism in an Authoritarian State
latest.abstract: Some have expressed concern that the Western concepts of constructive and solutions journalism could be used to silence critical journalists in countries with restrictions on media freedom. Using qualitative interviews, this study asked journalists in Rwanda if they believe solutions journalism is appropriate in their authoritarian media context. Findings indicate that although journalists like the idea of solutions journalism, they believe solutions stories will not benefit society if they cannot exist alongside stories that expose problems.

latest.title: Gender-Inclusive Language Shapes News Evaluations: An Experimental Study of the Effects on Perceived Credibility, Reactance, and Media Skepticism among News Users
latest.abstract: Gender-inclusive language (GIL) is increasingly used in journalism in many countries worldwide, yet its effects on news evaluations are largely unexplored. We conducted a preregistered online experiment with a sample representative of the adult German population (N = 812), manipulating linguistic form in two news articles on topics unrelated to gender: masculine-only form (e.g., “Bürger”), pair form (e.g., “Bürger und Bürgerinnen”), or star form (“Bürger*innen”). We expected that, depending on their attitude toward GIL, people would use GIL as a positive or negative credibility cue. Furthermore, as opponents tend to be deeply involved in the social conflict surrounding GIL, we expected GIL to trigger reactance and media skepticism among this group. Our findings revealed that the star form slightly influenced credibility, depending on attitude congruence. In addition, it triggered affective but not cognitive reactance among opponents and, unexpectedly, reduced their media skepticism. The pair form had no impact, likely because it is more common and less ideologically loaded. Theoretically, these results extend previous research on trust in journalism by suggesting that small linguistic cues indicating gender inclusivity can shape people’s evaluations of news articles.

latest.title: Selling War at Home and Abroad: The Dual Objective of State Media Propaganda in the Russo-Ukrainian War
latest.abstract: This study examines how authoritarian regimes set conflicting domestic and foreign propaganda agenda during wartime to ensure domestic unity and engage international audiences. We posit that authoritarian regimes relying on public support for legitimacy attempt to keep domestic opinion onside by emphasizing the high stakes and low costs of war, thereby ensuring that dissent against the conflict does not threaten the regime. Foreign audiences, on the other hand, are encouraged to consider their responsibility and the risks of catastrophic escalation associated with intervention. We test our argument by analyzing domestic and international Russian propaganda around the reinvasion of Ukraine from January 2022 to August 2023. By comparing war coverage tailored for domestic audiences in RIA Novosti and foreign-facing coverage that appeared on RT, we find greater emphasis on the threat from the opponent, the high stakes of the war, and less emphasis on risks in domestic media. Foreign media focuses more on international actors' responsibility, the local stakes, and the risks of nuclear escalation. We conclude with a discussion of our findings and the tradeoffs autocracies must contend with in the management of the media during wartime.

latest.title: Enthusiastic or Averse, Yet Nonchalant: Mapping Early-Career Journalists’ Engagement with Gen AI in Indian Newsrooms
Talking to China About Climate Change: How Non-profit Journalism Diversifies Climate News in China
latest.abstract: In pursuit of public service, a growing number of news non-profits are emerging worldwide to fill the gap in mainstream journalism and strengthen climate communication. Drawing on framing analysis of three non-profit news organisations – Dialogue Earth, Carbon Brief and Greenpeace – and comparing their climate coverage with Chinese mainstream journalism, this study examines how non-profit journalism with international background can contribute more diverse climate news to Chinese media landscape. While mainstream journalism largely follows the official line and highlights the country’s climate achievements, the non-profit outlets provide critical perspectives urging for stronger climate governance. Strategic framing helps their reporting adapt to China’s media environment, forming a deliberative critique that diverges from conventional watchdog journalism. While the conventional mode normally focuses on accountability and crisis, the non-profit outlets pay more attention to policy shortcomings through rational, expert-led deliberation. This underscores the need for further inquiry into how non-profit journalism can better inform the public on climate issues across contexts, and reaffirms the value of news framing as a lens for analysing nuanced forms of critical journalism.

latest.title: Fewer but More Elaborate: How Information Accessibility Filters Participation and Shapes Online News Comments
latest.abstract: Information accessibility in journalism operates along two dimensions that may work against each other: increasing information availability raises what news stories offer audiences, while simultaneously elevating the cognitive demands that determine whether audiences can use it. To test whether this gap functions as a participation filtering mechanism, we examine how four informational features, namely statistical information, external sources, data visualizations, and analytic style, are associated with participation volume and the linguistic structure of comments, using data journalism as the empirical context where this tension is most pronounced. Analyzing 6,400 New York Times stories and 934,992 comments from 2014 to 2022 through computational text analysis and structural equation modeling, we find that stories with higher information availability, particularly those with greater statistical information and analytic style, are associated with fewer but more analytically structured comments. Reduced participation mediates this relationship, suggesting that the availability and usability gap functions as an indirect pathway linking informational features to more elaborated audience responses. Stories published in the data journalism section show independently higher cognitive elaboration, pointing to a complementary self-selection pathway. The findings suggest that information accessibility is a structural condition of journalism that shapes not only audience engagement but who participates and how.

latest.title: Media Attention and Missing Persons Recovery: A National Analysis of Media Attention, Bias, and Victim Recovery
latest.abstract: The media is said to be a vital tool in the efforts to solve active missing person cases. Previous research indicates that not all cases receive equal amounts of attention in both the traditional and social media realms. This study is the first of its kind to empirically test the role of news media in the recovery of missing persons. Results suggest that traditional media attention significantly impacts the likelihood of victim recovery. Disparity and symmetry in media attention of missing persons cases were also found, for both traditional and social media. The circumstances of missingness appear to play a vital role in media attention and victim recovery. Policy implications related to missing persons case handling are discussed.

latest.title: Networks of Influence: Journalism Innovation and the Politics of Public Support
latest.abstract: In recent years innovation gained traction as a prominent policy rationale informing the design of publicly funded initiatives for journalism support. While this shift reflects the urgency of supporting structural transformation in the field, the processes through which such programmes are designed remain underexplored, particularly the role and configuration of influential stakeholders’ networks and the innovation rationales they help institutionalize. Through a case-study approach, this article investigates the design of a digital transformation programme for the Flemish media sector, a publicly funded initiative launched in 2022 and concluded in 2024. Grounded in Policy Network Theory and following Stakeholder and Advocacy Coalition Framework analysis, the study analyses through expert interviews (N = 23), how key stakeholders access and influence both the formulation of the programme and its prevailing innovation rationales. The findings reveal a stratified policy network, in which intermediary actors bridge a central policy core with an inner circle of influential stakeholders, while more peripheral actors remain loosely connected. These intermediaries facilitate both formal and informal agenda-setting, before and during the policy consultation phase. Finally, this study indicates that techno-centric imaginaries, shaped by platform logics, inform the policy framing, raising normative questions about inclusivity and long-term orientation in journalism innovation policy.

latest.title: When Attention Hurts: How Multimodal Sensational Frames Drive Both Engagement and Victim-Blaming in News on Gender-Based Violence
latest.abstract: This study examines how sensational strategies independently and interactively shape public attitudes. We conceptualize the sensational victim frame as a theoretical domain comprising two dimensions—victimization and objectifying—each manifested in textual and visual forms. The analysis is based on a dataset of 16,908 gender-based violence news posts and 279,652 associated comments from Weibo (2020–2024). Textual victimization and visual objectifying significantly increase user engagement. Moreover, these two strategies independently heighten the likelihood of victim-blaming comments, and their cross-modal combinations further amplify this effect. Overall, the findings demonstrate that sensationalism in gender-based violence reporting operates through distinct textual and visual pathways that can both attract and harm audiences. This study advances multimodal framing theory and offers practical implications for ethical reporting and platform design aimed at mitigating revictimization while sustaining public attention.

trending.title: AI in the Newsroom: Does the Public Trust Automated Journalism and Will They Pay for It?
trending.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being adapted for news production tasks in news outlets worldwide. Whether the public trusts news outlets relying on AI to produce news remains unclear. Further, the economic implications (willingness to pay and ad acceptance) and moderators remain unexplored. We conducted a pre-registered 2 × 2 experiment with a quota-based nonprobability sample from Germany (N = 1,261). Respondents were exposed to vignettes about a fictional online news outlet. We manipulated the production process (generative AI vs. trained journalists, between-subject) and the topic covered (politics vs. entertainment, within-subject). Participants trusted outlets with AI-generated news less, particularly political ones. They were less willing to accept seeing ads shown by AI outlets and outlets that covered entertainment. Willingness to pay was not affected. We explored moderators: Individuals with the perception that AIs spread incorrect information were less trusting in AI-generated news. These perceptions did not moderate the relationship with willingness to pay or ad acceptance. The opinion climate did not moderate the effect of the content production process. In sum, AI in the newsroom may decrease trust and ad revenue of outlets. This effect might be exacerbated depending on audience characteristics. We discuss implications for theory, future scholarship, and media organizations.

trending.title: Knowledge Silos as a Barrier to Responsible AI Practices in Journalism? Exploratory Evidence from Four Dutch News Organisations
trending.abstract: The effective adoption of responsible AI practices in journalism requires a concerted effort to bridge different perspectives, including technological, editorial, and managerial. Among the many challenges that could impact information sharing around responsible AI inside news organisations are knowledge silos, where information is isolated within one part of the organisation and not easily shared with others. This study aims to study how knowledge silos might affect the adoption of responsible AI practices in journalism through a cross-case study of four Dutch media outlets. We examine individual and organisational barriers to AI knowledge sharing and the extent to which knowledge silos could impede the operationalisation of responsible AI initiatives inside these newsrooms. To address this question, we conducted 14 semi-structured interviews with a strategic sample of editors, managers, and journalists at de Telegraaf, de Volkskrant, NOS, and RTL Nederland. The interviews aimed to uncover insights into the existence of knowledge silos, their effects on responsible AI practice adoption, and the organisational practices influencing these dynamics. Our results emphasise the importance of creating better structures for sharing information on AI across all layers of news organisations and highlight the need for research on knowledge silos as an impediment to responsible AI production.

trending.title: Journalism and Embodied Knowledge: Conceptualizing Affective Epistemology and Epistemic Affordances of Emotions and Affect Across News Beats
trending.abstract: This conceptual paper aims to theorize the role of journalists’ bodies in knowledge-making practices by focusing on affects and emotions as a mediatrix of biological, social, and political bodies. It does so by developing the concepts of journalists’ “affective epistemology” and “epistemic affordances” of emotions and affect that, altogether, aim to provide journalism researchers with a conceptual toolkit for studying the role of emotions and affect in journalistic epistemology. The notion of affective epistemology is based on (1) relevant empirical research on journalism, emotions, and affect, (2) Feminist Standpoint Epistemology, and (3) selected philosophical, sociological, and anthropological theories of emotions and embodied knowledge. The paper also identifies five epistemic affordances of emotions and affect in journalism, i.e., ways how they can be illuminating as well as blinding in journalists’ knowledge-building and fact-finding practices: motivational, methodological-analytical, ontological-narrative, collaborative-innovative, and phatic-interactional. Examples illustrating these affordances come from existing research on various journalism beats, from lifestyle and cultural journalism to conflict reporting. In conclusion, I ask how journalists can integrate emotions in knowledge-building practices in a way that makes emotions rather illuminating than blinding. I suggest that a productive use of emotions/affects requires maximum reflexivity, virtue responsibility, and emotional literacy.

trending.title: Fact-Checking in Journalism: An Epistemological Framework
trending.abstract: Fact-checking has become an enduring form of journalism that can influence public discussion and counter false content on mass media and social media platforms. However, communication scholars have questioned some epistemological premises of fact-checking and their embeddedness in journalistic practices. This study examines the validity of this criticism by defining three deep-rooted challenges threatening to compromise the epistemological basis of fact-checking. We analysed the problems related to degrees of objectivism, truth regimes, and causal relations across five different aspects of fact-checking to trace where epistemological concerns originate and how they can be resolved. Consequently, we provide a set of measures (rigour, presentation, and audience engagement) that can be used to explore the nature of epistemological problems in fact-checking contexts. We argue that these measures can support and reinforce the epistemological foundations of fact-checking if they are applied in a way that transparently recognises the subjective elements included in fact-checking work. Recognition of subjective elements is essential when developing novel and existing fact-checking methods, given the risks of bias replication and subjectivity in AI-powered systems and other technological solutions.

trending.title: “I Feel It in My Body, in My Soul, in My Mind”: Journalism, Racist News and Immigrants’ Experience of Belonging
trending.abstract: We know that journalism, and particularly news, has an essential function in society and politics and that it shapes our understanding of reality. Yet, we fail to recognize its far-reaching implications on the lived experience of those who consume it. This article contributes towards addressing this gap by examining the response of individuals with an immigrant background to racist representations of immigrants in Norwegian news during the Covid-19 pandemic. It involved 21 in-depth interviews that mapped how the coverage both was entwined with and refracted through the participants’ emotions, embodied and situated experiences, impacting their sense of belonging in Norwegian society. The analysis demonstrates the devastating reverberations of racist news discourse on all domains of an immigrant’s life: far from merely providing information, news profoundly affects an immigrant’s sense of safety, health and well-being, and feeling (or not) “at home.” The study has relevance beyond the Norwegian case and the timeframe of the pandemic in so far as it moves beyond existing research about “news effects” and “audience studies.” Theoretically it conceptualizes news as both elemental and existential. Methodologically, it approaches it as woven into the experience of immigrants rather than as an external influence on it.

trending.title: Beyond Journalism About Journalism?: Assessing the Impact of Metajournalistic Discourse on Journalism Studies
trending.abstract: This article presents a systematic review of the literature examining metajournalistic discourse, a term proposed by Carlson to encompass all public utterances about the nature and boundaries of journalism. After collecting all scholarly output (N = 77) between 2015 and 2023, a content analysis of the articles was conducted, with particular attention paid to two key areas: the components (actors, sites/audiences, and topics) and interpretive processes (definitional control, boundary-work, and legitimation) of discourse. Our findings allow us to make a number of observations regarding the current state of research: 1) the study of metajournalistic discourse is dominated by a Western bias; 2) research approaches remain journalist-centric; 3) boundary-work concerns above all the relationship of journalism to technology and market imperatives; 4) the democratic/societal role of journalism emerges as the main legitimation strategy; 5) the topics of metajournalistic discourse have organic and prompted origins.

trending.title: Bringing Up the Body: Uncovering the Subjectivity of Journalists
trending.abstract: In this paper, I discuss major contributions to journalism studies that come from approaching journalistic practice from the vantage point of the body – that is, understanding how journalists go about their work in ways shaped by their embodied experience. I will develop the argument that a consideration of the journalistic body requires a challenge to the fundamental underpinnings of professional practice, which are premised on the invisibility of the body. Foregrounding the body in relation to journalism practice calls for greater reflexivity in relation to the subjectivity of journalists. The paper discusses three overlapping insights resulting from such an approach: First, it requires attention to individual journalists’ bodies and lived experience in relation to their pasts – or what journalists “carry.” Second, it calls for attention to how they feel in the present – and how these affective responses shape their practice. Finally, it requires charting how journalists’ bodies interact with other bodies, and the institutions surrounding them, as they go about their work.

trending.title: Thriving in Journalism: A Survey of Support Systems’ Impact on Job Satisfaction and Well-Being
trending.abstract: Journalists rely on a patchwork of support from organizational, institutional, and interpersonal sources, about which the academic literature has growing evidence. Building on this literature, this study seeks to provide such an overview, while also asking how well these patchwork supports function. A nationally representative survey of 633 U.S. reporters finds that trust in management and a supportive workplace culture are most important for journalists’ job satisfaction; work–life balance and support from family and friends are most important for journalists’ overall well-being. Income was a strong predictor of both job satisfaction and well-being. Overall, results point to the important role of editors as creators of workplace culture and front-line caregivers, suggesting a need for management training.

trending.title: On Controlled Change: Generative AI’s Impact on Professional Authority in Journalism
trending.abstract: Using (generative) artificial intelligence tools and systems in journalism is expected to increase journalists’ production rates, transform newsrooms’ economic models, and further personalize the audience’s news consumption practices. Since its release in 2022, OpenAI’s ChatGPT and other large language models have raised alarms within news organizations, not only for introducing new challenges to news reporting and fact-checking but also for what these technologies would mean for journalists’ professional authority. This paper examines how journalists in Dutch media integrate AI technologies into their daily routines. Drawing on 13 interviews with editors, journalists, and innovation managers across different news outlets and media companies, we use controlled change as an interpretative frame derived from empirical data to explain how journalists are proactively setting guidelines, experimenting with AI tools, and identifying their limitations and capabilities. Using professional authority as a theoretical framework, we argue that journalists anticipate and integrate AI technologies in a supervised manner and identify three primary mechanisms through which journalists manage this integration: (1) developing adaptive guidelines that align AI use with ethical codes, (2) experimenting with AI technologies to determine their necessity and fit, and (3) critically assessing the capabilities and limitations of AI systems.

trending.title: “journalists are just employees”: Examining Journalistic Autonomy from an Audience Perspective
trending.abstract: Autonomy is a fundamental requirement for the professional practice of journalism. However, while its role in ensuring well-informed audiences is widely acknowledged, the way in which audiences make sense of journalists’ autonomy remains unexplored. Similarly, the understanding of how audience perceptions of journalists’ autonomy, their attributed professionalism and authority, and the resulting impact on journalism practice remains incomplete. To address these gaps, this study conducts a qualitative analysis involving semi-structured interviews with 64 news users in Chile. Results show that journalists’ autonomy, from audiences’ view, is limited by labor forces and organizational influences. Journalists’ working conditions are perceived to be connected to high levels of editorial control, yielding a deficiency of autonomy that relegates journalists to a subservient role, compromising their professionalism, undermining their authority, and eroding the quality of the information they provide. Also, findings show that autonomy assumes a prominent role as a distinct form of authority when journalists diverge from conventional news norms, establishing a closer connection with their audience. Furthermore, independent journalists frequently garner recognition for their autonomy and credibility, attributed to their detachment from specific media outlets. The article delves into the implications of these findings for journalism studies and practice.

trending.title: Whose Voices Shape Protest Narratives? Comparing Source Diversity in Kenya’s Digital-Native and Legacy-Affiliated News Coverage
trending.abstract: This study investigates the construction of protest narratives in online-only and legacy-affiliated digital news media, specifically examining their sourcing practices during Kenya’s 2024 anti-Finance Bill protests. By analyzing the digital-native outlet Kenyans.co.ke alongside the legacy outlet Citizen Digital, the research reveals significant yet subtle differences in source diversity. Both platforms primarily depend on authoritative voices, with government officials making up 32% of sources in each outlet. However, Kenyans.co.ke provides slightly more representation for protesters and activists (27.7% vs. 23.9%) and the general public (16.9% vs. 14.9%), along with a greater reliance on social media sources (9.2% vs. 7.5%). These findings indicate that digital-native platforms may afford a somewhat wider array of grassroots perspectives, though neither outlet substantially diverges from the dominance of official sources. This study highlights a critical tension in protest coverage: while digital platforms open avenues for diverse voices, institutional narratives continue to prevail. By examining these continuities and disruptions, the research enriches discussions about media democratization, the limitations of journalistic practices, and the potential for alternative sourcing to transform protest narratives. It calls for a deeper examination of how both legacy and digital media architectures either reinforce or challenge existing power dynamics in public discourse.

trending.title: Decoding Correction Strategies: How Fact-Checkers Uncover Falsehoods Across Countries
trending.abstract: This study systematically analyzes and compares verification strategies employed by fact-checking organizations across various contexts. Utilizing a dataset of 3,154 verification articles from 23 organizations in eight countries across Europe and Latin America, the study identifies 17 distinct debunking techniques through both inductive and deductive approaches. The primary objectives are to uncover common and divergent practices in factual correction, assess how techniques vary by verification target (e.g., online rumors versus statements by public figures), and examine variations at organizational and national levels. The findings reveal that while methods such as providing documents and tracing misinformation origins are prevalent, significant variation exists depending on the target. For online rumors, common practices include tracing misinformation origins, forensic analysis, and visual indicators of image manipulation. Conversely, verification of public figure statements frequently involves expert arbitration and direct contact with misinformation sources. Additionally, the study highlights substantial differences in fact-checking strategies across countries and organizations, influenced by their focus and institutional contexts. This research addresses a notable gap in the literature by offering a comparative analysis of verification strategies, providing a framework for future experimental research, and offering guidance for fact-checkers and scholars to refine their approaches to combating misinformation.

trending.title: Is Press Freedom Better Protected in Democracies? Internet Shutdown and Journalism in India
trending.abstract: It's commonly assumed that democracies are comparatively better than non-democratic regimes in safeguarding press freedom from political interference and ensuring constitutional and regulatory safeguards. Although this perception is largely true, numerous recent examples have shown journalism coming under attack in democratic regimes too. Drawing upon qualitative interviews conducted with journalists during and after the world's longest internet shutdown in the state of Jammu and Kashmir in India in 2019, this article underscores the measures used by the Indian government to control the flow of information. The article unpacks the dynamics of reporting by local, national and international media during the internet shutdown and shows how differing perceptions of their roles allowed journalists to perform their professional tasks even in difficult situations. Given the fact that repression of journalistic freedom occurred in a democracy, and at a time when the world is more connected than before, this not only challenges the normative understanding of how journalism functions in democracies but it may also hold lessons for journalists in circumventing the use of such tactics in other democracies.

trending.title: On Being a Good Worker, a Good Mother, a Good Carer: Women Journalists, Motherhood, and Caregiving
trending.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between journalism, caregiving, and family-building, focusing on women journalists in Portugal. Drawing on a critical thematic analysis of thirty interviews, it explores an analytic framework that includes cultural, structural, and agentic dimensions of career limitations, organised in three overarching themes. The first examines how women journalists experience work constraints stemming from traditional cultural ideals where women are still the main caregivers and work cultures that perpetuate a male perspective on professional routines. The second theme explores the mismatch between work and care responsibilities that arises from prevailing family structures and work processes. The third theme centres on how women journalists respond to constraints by making choices and developing strategies. Journalists’ reflexive deliberations about career decisions, employment conditions, family life and cultural assumptions underpinning parenthood demonstrate the complex interrelationship between cultural and working structures, organisational materiality, and agency. Together, these dimensions replicate patterns that make journalism more inhospitable for women. A central point in this research is that while a systemic gender bias exists beyond the sector, workplace inequalities are particularly consequential for journalism and democracy.

trending.title: News on TikTok Through the Lens of Quality Journalism: How TikTok Users Perceive News Values, Content, and Engagement
trending.abstract: As TikTok becomes an increasingly popular platform for news consumption, it is important to understand how its unique format aligns with or challenges traditional journalistic standards. This study draws on the quality journalism framework, which consists of professional norms, content features, and audience engagement dimensions, to examine how U.S. TikTok users perceive the quality of news they encounter on the platform. Based on in-depth interviews with 23 TikTok news users, we find that while entertainment is a main motivation for using TikTok, users still value traditional journalistic principles such as information utility, accuracy, and credibility. Users express different expectations for news quality depending on the news topic and the source, whether the content comes from influencers or legacy media. Many users view TikTok news as an entry point to learning about current events and often seek out additional information on other platforms. Our findings suggest that users expect TikTok journalism to maintain a balance between engaging presentation and journalistic rigor. This study contributes to the growing literature on TikTok journalism by focusing on audience perspectives and offering a nuanced look at how news quality is understood within the TikTok context.

trending.title: Bodying the War Correspondent: Deploying Creative Practice to Explore the Reporter's Body as a Sense-Making Tool
trending.abstract: In her 2021 essay, Bodying the Journalist, Chantal Francoeur acknowledges that journalists’ bodily experiences – “that complex assemblage of impulses, reactions, senses, emotions, energies and physical states” – are not easy to categorise or analyse. She argues that foregrounding the body both as an object of study and as a key resource for conducting research lies in part with journalists themselves investigating how they use their bodies as sense-making tools. This article operationalises Francoeur's three-dimensional framework for understanding how journalists deploy their bodies through the creation and analysis of a personal essay about the lived experience of a Reuters staff correspondent who was assigned to Afghanistan in 2011. The essay was written by one of the authors in journalism's creative non-fiction genre to explore her everyday encounters and embodied routines during a key period in the conflict that saw a surge in violence and coincided with the major news event of Osama Bin Laden's death. The personal essay's focus on how the journalist mobilised her body in her daily encounters with the new environment and interactions with others contributes to growing recognition of the emotional and physical work performed behind news headlines.

trending.title: Reflecting, Regulating, Adapting: Metacognition’s Role in Journalism Practices
trending.abstract: This article advances our understanding of transparency in journalism through the lens of metacognition. Drawing on a six-week intervention with eight U.S. newsrooms, the study analyzes journalists’ reflective journals using the Eight Pillars of Metacognition and a three-stage interpretive method. Findings reveal that journalists used metacognitive strategies—such as self-monitoring, adaptation, discrimination, and mnemosyne—to question assumptions, revise workflows, and embed transparency into daily practice. Rather than treating transparency as a discrete output or static ideal, this study positions it as a situated epistemic practice that unfolds through internal reflection, institutional memory, and relational ethics. While existing scholarship critiques transparency’s limited impact on public trust, this article argues that its unrealized potential lies in how it is practiced and internalized. Metacognition offers a conceptual bridge between normative ideals and newsroom work’s messy, iterative realities. This reorientation from transparency-as-disclosure to transparency-as-reflection highlights the cognitive labor journalists perform to remain accountable in uncertain and constrained environments. The study contributes to journalism studies by theorizing metacognition as both a professional resource and a democratic imperative that equips journalists to navigate audience skepticism, institutional pressures, and the evolving demands of ethical practice.

trending.title: “The View from the Top”: Elite Metajournalistic Responses to Normative Critiques of American Journalism
trending.abstract: Recent debates about journalism’s abiding values have often centered the role journalistic objectivity has played in sustaining various inequities in American society. Amid these challenges, newsroom leaders, executives, and owners have spoken publicly about a need to defend the profession’s traditions, especially a commitment to objectivity and independence. Through a textual analysis of arguments and statements from top editors and publishers defending values like objectivity and independence, this study considers how a form of metajournalistic discourse has emerged from journalism’s managerial class that rhetorically and ideologically moderates calls for cultural change from both inside and outside the profession. As elite figures define threats to the field—externally from rising authoritarianism and inwardly from a generation questioning traditional values—they proffer a return to independence, setting boundaries around critiques calling for ethical and normative change, but also preserving an elite insularity that has long been part of journalism’s professional culture.

trending.title: Covering Environment and Climate Change in Turkey: Transformative Journalisms Face Competitive Authoritarianism
trending.abstract: As the climate crisis deepens, journalistic interventions aimed at engaging citizens with news that raises public awareness and promotes climate solutions are gaining significance throughout the globe. Drawing on the conceptual framework of transformative journalisms, this study focuses on professional discourses, practices, emotions, and challenges of climate journalists in Turkey to improve our understanding of their operations in a highly polarized and oppressive political atmosphere. The research is based on qualitative, in-depth interviews with 21 journalists from different regions of Turkey who identified as climate journalists or environmental journalists prioritizing the climate crisis. The findings suggest that journalists go beyond solely reporting on climate science and undertake the mission of advocacy for the transformation toward ecological sustainability despite constant political oppression, financial restraints, and polarization traps. Although inspiring hardly any policy change under the circumstances demotivates the journalists, niche outlets invest in raising community-level awareness of climate change and forging broad alliances with local journalists, actors of environmental movements, and civil society, keeping hopes alive for bottom-up transformation. The most urgent needs are dedicated training programs for emergent journalists, generating sustainable income models, and challenging the discourse of pro-government media through local stories with a climate angle.

trending.title: What “Digital Literacies” Must Journalists Have? Unpacking How Journalists Define and Practice News Literacy, Data Literacy, and Algorithmic and AI Literacy in the Digital Age
trending.abstract: As media environments become increasingly complex, with a myriad of actors producing news, new technologies entering into newsrooms, and a large amount of data and (fake) news in circulation, journalists must obtain a set of “digital literacies” essential to function in the newsroom. Such literacies will enable journalists to perform their public service role to accurately inform the citizenry; currently, journalist perspectives on this topic have never been explored. Through in-depth interviews with journalists and editors, this study reveals “news literacy”, “data literacy”, “algorithmic literacy” and “AI literacy” as core to contemporary journalistic work—participants in this study offered their own definitions of these terms, and how these literacies are put into practice as actual newsroom behaviors, such as research, verification, diversification of sources, contextualization of data, and search engine optimization. Given obstacles such as time constraints, unfamiliarity with new technologies, and the presence of certain beliefs and discourses that might hinder the practice of such literacies, this paper points to two factors that can encourage such literacy behaviors—pertaining to (1) personal motivations and (2) organizational norms and structures—to increase journalistic knowledge and skills in the digital age.

trending.title: Bodies in Journalism: The View from Behind and in Front of the Lens
trending.abstract: Perhaps nowhere is the importance of the body more keenly felt than in visual journalism. With precious few exceptions, journalists who use cameras to produce journalism can’t “call it in” and must be physically on the scene to do their jobs. This comes with unique implications for how these journalists regulate their bodies and perform their roles. But, in the past two decades, the visual side of journalism has been gutted. Fewer staff photojournalists are employed, and the slack is increasingly being taken up by words-based reporters who must also make images in addition to their other duties and by so-called “citizen photojournalists” whose vision, sometimes shared on social media, journalists integrate into their reporting. Acknowledging these dynamics, this study explores within the context of Australia the types of bodies that are making visual news in regional, rural, or remote settings, how bodies are being represented in visual news in these areas, and how the embodied nature of visual journalism affects the way that news images are made and presented. The results reveal a great deal about how the body is valued—or devalued—in visual journalism and provides insights for scholars and practitioners alike.

trending.title: The Somatechnics of Journalism: Applying an Embodied Perspective to Enduring Issues in Journalism Studies
trending.abstract: This research applies Somatechnics to the study of journalism and contributes to an emergent epistemological “bodily turn” in the discipline of Journalism Studies. This is a turn toward the body, embodied experience, and the inevitable emotionality of journalism and the journalist as brought forth by Chantal Francoeur and Belinda Middleweek, among others. We invite journalism scholars (and practitioners) to understand journalists’ bodies as sophisticated organic technologies—and to subsequently understand how those bodies are further transmogrified by, and collapsed into, the ever-changing world of news media. We deploy a process of retheorising as a qualitative method in which researchers apply new theoretical frameworks to existing studies or data to provide fresh insights and perspectives. By doing so, we offer a Somatechnics of Journalism as one of several emerging conceptual frameworks to help us turn to the body in Journalism Studies.

trending.title: Presenting America Through the Translation Gate: A Case Study of Reference News on the WeChat Public Account Platform
trending.abstract: Translation has rarely been the analytical focus in communication and journalism studies, which might be ascribed to an outdated understanding of the term “translation.” This study highlighted the crucial role of the translation gate in curating news narratives. It adopts an extended conceptualization of journalistic translation, which considers translation in news production as a two-level gatekeeping practice. Specifically, this study aimed to investigate translation’s gatekeeping function at the macro level. To this end, popular translated news reports covering the United States posted in 2020 on the WeChat account of an official Chinese media outlet, Reference News (RN), were collected. By employing content analysis, this study scrutinized the sources used, topics covered, and story tones of the collected reports. The findings indicate that RN exhibited a preference for established and pro-China media sources in covering the United States. The topics in the examined reports were mostly hard news with a few instances of soft news. While the majority of news reports were negative, positive stories were also identified, demonstrating RN’s efforts to disseminate constructive journalism.

trending.title: Disruptions in Normalization: Reflexive Monitoring in Journalism Adaptation and Audience Collaboration
trending.abstract: In the adaptation of innovations, journalists often reflect on areas of concern that can lead to subsequent selection, a strategic process of diminishing the practice of a routine. Through the lens of normalization process theory and structuration theory, this article explores how journalists reflexively monitor innovations. The article also elaborates on the ways journalists evaluate disruptive circumstances that can lead them to select routines for denormalization. Using 44 interviews with journalists from the United States, this study argues that reflexive monitoring occurs through collaborations with audiences: a key to helping re-center journalists on the viability of a routine with existing commitments.

trending.title: Broadcasting through the (New) Iron Curtain: Practices, Challenges, and Legacies of Russia's Independent Media in Exile
trending.abstract: The Russo-Ukrainian war and the Kremlin's military censorship have made independent reporting from within Russia impossible. After a few weeks of the conflict, all institutional journalism was forced into exile. Funding sources, access to informants, and the ability to provide objective conflict coverage quickly vanished. Now in exile, Russian journalists have become entirely reliant on donor funding to sustain operations and on new technologies to reach audiences inside Russia. Over 18 months in exile, we conducted more than 50 interviews with editors-in-chief, senior correspondents, and individual journalists adapting to these new circumstances. We asked about audience access, funding opportunities, reliance on new technologies, and organisational challenges within newsrooms. This paper argues that these new conditions have underscored pre-existing issues within Russian media while introducing challenges brought about by the war and exile. However, in a global context, these issues closely mirror those faced by exiled journalists worldwide.

trending.title: How Journalists Deal with Inclusion and Objectivity: Three Models of Social Justice Coverage
trending.abstract: This article investigates how journalists perceive the role of inclusion and objectivity in their coverage of social justice topics. Theoretically, this article engages with the concept of objectivity through the feminist lens of standpoint theory. Seventeen semi-structured interviews were conducted with journalists covering LGBTI topics, nine of whom identified as non-heterosexual, from five prominent Flemish newspapers. The findings reveal three distinct approaches to covering social justice issues, based on how journalists conceptualize objectivity and inclusion in their work: the objectivity model, the inclusivity model, and the advocacy model. Additionally, this article identifies three key challenges to achieving more inclusive coverage that go beyond the traditional notion of objectivity: implementing clear guidelines, fostering reflexivity, and addressing intersectional shortcomings. Newsrooms can tackle these challenges by creating opportunities for reflection, both in terms of time and physical space, and by openly communicating their value frameworks to both audiences and staff. This is particularly crucial in an era marked by deliberate provocations against LGBTI rights.

trending.title: Competing for Cultural Authority: Journalism Studies Must Account for the Right
trending.abstract: Recent technological and political developments have caused researchers to reevaluate journalists’ relevance vis a vis other forms of media production, with some calling for a “decentering” of journalism within broader media cultures. While there has been sizeable growth in research concerning the impacts of new digital technologies on journalism, we call for a renewed focus on partisan media. We contend that the future of journalism studies necessarily involves a reckoning with right-wing news cultures and note four areas where further research is especially necessary: including theorizing how conservative news influences and its epistemological assumptions, as well as right-wing media’s increasing salience across a diverse array of communities in the U.S. and across the globe. We intend this essay as a provocation to journalism studies scholars, with the goal of effecting a robust and reflexive subfield devoted to the study of right-wing news.

trending.title: Examining Journalists’ Adoption of Social Media Tools in Contexts of Precarity
trending.abstract: Digital technologies have changed journalists’ work practices and their roles with far-reaching effects for news production. While many studies focus on the ways social media transforms editorial processes, much of this research examines fully democratic Western countries. We examine how journalists in Turkey, who occupy particularly precarious social positions, incorporate social media tools into their routines, and the effects of these tools on journalistic role conceptions. To understand this, we analyzed 10 interviews with Turkish editors and reporters from popular Turkish news outlets. These journalists say their roles are shifting from active news formation to passive information relay — they are becoming aggregators rather than reporters. And while social networking sites increase the volume of newsworthy ideas that journalists encounter, they also increase the pressure on editors and reporters to compete with other news outlets. The organizations we studied did not employ separate fact-checking teams or software for news verification, leading to workflow challenges around verifying large quantities of information collected from social media. Our findings suggest that journalists in precarious positions might be especially reliant on social media logics in their daily work since they lack the social, political, and occupational security to improvise or resist new practices and values.
